name: Priya Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Priya. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the demand planning team at Brightway, a big home-improvement chain with about three hundred stores. My team of six works out how many tins of paint, drills and bags of compost each store needs every week, so the shelves are full but the warehouses aren't. Mornings are dashboards and a call with the buyers, and afternoons are fixing whatever the weather has done to the forecast.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where does AI fit into your day right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Everywhere, honestly. I use an AI assistant every day to draft the weekly order notes and explain odd numbers, and last spring I built a little tool that flags stores selling out early. Helen, my boss, calls me the team's early adopter, which is half a compliment. Some of my team are less keen, and Olu in particular thinks I'm automating us out of a job.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I married Tomasz last year. He's an electrician working for a contractor on new housing estates, so he's up at six and I'm up at seven. We rent a flat ten minutes from my parents' bakery, I still help there the odd Saturday, and we go to Mass with my parents on Sundays. We've got about three months of costs saved, and we want a house and children within a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, gently, to the people who said it would replace everyone. It's a good tool and I'll keep using it, but it's a tool. Online I'd probably post a joke about all the conferences that will need new themes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a little disappointed, because I'd hoped my early start would set me apart. If nothing big happens, being good with AI is just a nice skill, like being good with spreadsheets. My job's safe either way and Brightway's doing fine, so I'd mostly go back to worrying about house prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building small tools for the team, like extending the sell-out alert to garden furniture next spring. I'd teach Olu and the others to draft their weekly notes with the assistant, so it isn't just me. And Tomasz and I would keep putting five hundred a month aside for the house deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit flat, maybe, like a big match that ends nil-nil. But nothing about my work or our money would feel at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said house prices are the real worry. How big a worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Real but manageable. Prices near my parents went up again this year, and we'd need about another eighteen months of saving to get a deposit together. It's the normal worry everyone our age has, not something keeping me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Olu thinks you're automating the team out of a job. In this world, would Olu be right?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I hope not. In this world the tools take the boring parts, like copying numbers between reports, and Olu gets more time for the stores that actually need a human to ring them. I'd want Olu to see AI as a helper rather than a threat.

say: I'd say a gentle **told you so** to people who said AI would replace everyone.
It's a **good tool** and I'll keep using it, but it's only a tool.
think: I'd be a little **disappointed**, because I hoped starting early would set me apart.
My job is **safe** and Brightway is fine, so house prices stay my main worry.
do: **Extend** my sell-out alert tool to garden furniture next spring.
**Teach** Olu and the team to draft weekly notes with the assistant.
**Keep saving** 500 a month with Tomasz for a house deposit.
feel: **Calm**, a bit flat, like a big match that ends nil-nil.
S0.quote: If nothing big happens, being good with AI is just a nice skill, like being good with spreadsheets.
fieldNote: Her only real pressure here is **house prices**, about eighteen months of saving from a deposit.
Slight **disappointment** suggests she has tied part of her identity to being early with AI.
Wants a sceptical colleague to see AI as a **helper**, and plans to teach rather than replace.

steps.text: Extend the store sell-out alert to garden furniture next spring
Teach the team to draft weekly order notes with the assistant
Save 500 a month with Tomasz towards a house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the biggest change in planning since barcodes, and the teams that take it on early will do best. At work I'd say it out loud in the team meeting, because I'd rather people hear it from me than from a restructure email. I'd also say the company has a duty to retrain its people, not just replace them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, forecasting is exactly the sort of thinking work this card describes, so my team of six could become two or three. I think I'd be one who stays, because I'm the one building the tools. But I'd be the manager who made the case for the cuts, and that sits badly with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd offer Helen a plan to automate the weekly store orders, with me leading it, before someone at head office does it worse. I'd push for the people whose work shrinks to move into store support or supplier roles, not out the door. And I'd put my next pay rise straight into an index fund, because if AI is this big I want a small slice of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and guilty at the same time. I'd enjoy the work, honestly, and I'd hate the conversations. My stomach would turn a little every time I saw Olu in the kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Olu?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Olu the honest version: the order-writing part of the job is going, and I'd fight for a store support role if that's wanted. Olu has two kids, and I'd hate to be the reason that household is worried. I'd rather be blunt early than kind and late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You lean towards free markets and people standing on their own feet. Does asking the company to retrain people sit easily with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, actually. I'm not asking for handouts, I'm asking the company to keep its side of a bargain. People gave Brightway years of hard work, and in my family, when you've had someone's loyalty, you look after them.

say: This is the **biggest change** in planning since barcodes, and early teams will do best.
Brightway has a **duty to retrain** its people, not just replace them.
think: Forecasting is pure **thinking work**, so my team of six could become two or three.
I'd likely **stay**, since I build the tools, but I'd be the one making the case for cuts.
do: **Pitch** Helen a plan to automate weekly store orders, with me leading it.
**Push** for affected staff to move into store support or supplier roles.
**Invest** my next pay rise in an index fund.
feel: **Excited and guilty** at once: I'd enjoy the work and hate the conversations.
S1.quote: I'd rather be blunt early than kind and late.
fieldNote: Her own job looks **safe** because she's the automator; the unease is about colleagues.
Reconciles free-market views with retraining as **keeping a bargain**, not a handout.
Already plans to **own a slice** of the change through an index fund.

steps.text: Propose and lead automating the weekly store orders this month
Put the next pay rise into an index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when we find out what people are for, and family, faith and community matter more than ever. At work I'd say it calmly and quickly: start planning now. Online, nothing, because everyone would be shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think being early with AI buys me about a year, not a career. By 2028 the thing doing my job doesn't need me to drive it. Tomasz is the safer earner in our house now, because robots that can wire houses come around 2031, and that's a strange thing to admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Tomasz that week and plan for him to go out on his own as an electrician, with me running the business side: quotes, bookings and invoices, using AI for all of it. I'd keep my Brightway salary as long as it lasts and put every spare pound into a fund for his van and tools. We'd stop eating out and push the house back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy-anxious, not frozen. I'd feel the clock ticking. I'd also feel oddly lucky to have married a man who works with his hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens around 2031, when the robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the part I can't answer. Three years of a good electrical business would let us save hard and maybe buy a small house, but I don't know what Tomasz does after robots can wire houses. I'd rather have three years of something than nothing, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, at Sunday lunch after Mass. My dad would say the bakery has survived supermarkets and it'll survive this, and he might be right, because people still like buying bread from a person. I'd offer to put the bakery's orders and accounts on AI tools too, so my parents save some hours.

say: This is when we learn **what people are for**; family, faith and community matter more.
At work I'd say it calmly: **start planning now**.
think: Being early with AI buys me **about a year**, not a career.
Tomasz is now the **safer earner**, since robots that wire houses come around 2031.
do: **Plan** with Tomasz that week for his own electrical firm, with me running the office.
**Keep** my Brightway salary and save every spare pound for his **van and tools**.
**Stop** eating out and push the house purchase back.
feel: **Busy-anxious**, not frozen, with the clock ticking.
Oddly **lucky** to have married someone who works with his hands.
S2.quote: I think being early with AI buys me about a year, not a career.
fieldNote: She quickly accepts her **own job** goes and turns to the household's hands-on earner.
Her plan buys **three years** and she admits she has no answer for after 2031.
Feels in control because she has a **concrete plan**, so anxious rather than alarmed.

steps.text: Set up an electrical firm with Tomasz, running its quotes and invoices
Save every spare pound for Tomasz's van and tools
Push the house purchase back until the firm is running

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if you start now, and I'd say it to my team on day one. I'd probably run a lunchtime session on what AI can already do, so nobody's guessing. I'd tell friends to learn something real alongside their day job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is almost the ideal amount of time for someone like me. I can get a promotion out of the automation work in the next two years, save hard, and still build something with Tomasz before 2031. The danger is that I enjoy the corporate work too much and leave it too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the head of planning role when it opens next year and use the bigger salary to save eight months of costs. In 2028 I'd help Tomasz register his own electrical firm and buy a van, and by 2030 I'd leave Brightway to run the office side full time. I'd also study for a bookkeeping qualification at night, so I'm not making it up as I go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but energised. It's like a work deadline you can see on the calendar. I'd also feel a bit sad about leaving a job I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might leave it too late. What would stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Comfort, mostly. A good salary and a nice title are hard to walk away from, especially if Brightway keeps promoting whoever automates everything. I'd write the leaving date down and tell Tomasz, so he holds me to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And children? You said you wanted them within a few years.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still try, maybe in 2029, once the business has its first year behind it. My mum had me while running the bakery, and I'd rather do it that way than wait for a perfect moment that never comes. Family isn't something I'd postpone for a computer.

say: Five years is **plenty** if you start now, and I'd tell my team on day one.
I'd run a **lunchtime session** on what AI can already do.
think: Five years is nearly **ideal** for me: promotion, savings, then a business with Tomasz.
The danger is enjoying corporate work too much and **leaving too late**.
do: **Go for** head of planning next year and save eight months of costs.
**Help** Tomasz register his firm and buy a van in 2028, then leave Brightway by 2030.
**Study** bookkeeping at night so I can run the office properly.
feel: **Nervous but energised**, like a deadline visible on the calendar.
A little **sad** about leaving a job I'm good at.
S3.quote: Family isn't something I'd postpone for a computer.
fieldNote: Her own role still ends by 2031, but a **written plan** gives her a strong sense of control.
She names her own **comfort** as the main risk, which is unusually self-aware.
Won't delay **children**, citing her mother running the bakery while raising her.

steps.text: Leave Brightway by 2030 to run the electrical firm's office
Save eight months of costs from a head of planning salary
Study for a bookkeeping qualification at night
Help Tomasz register his firm and buy a van in 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where nobody has an excuse. Ten years is two career moves for someone my age. I'd say it at work as a challenge, not a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years looks good for me, and I feel a bit guilty saying it. There'll be a decade of companies needing people who know how to bring AI in without wrecking their teams, and that's exactly what I do now. The real worry is 2039, when robots reach Tomasz's trade and we're both in our forties with kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in corporate work and aim to move into an AI rollout role, maybe at a consultancy, within three years, because that's where the pay would be. We'd buy a house in 2028 and try for our first child the same year. And I'd start a pension top-up now and put a share of every bonus into it, because 2039 needs money waiting for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly positive, with a worry tucked away at the back. I'd feel like the wind is behind me for once. The worry comes back whenever I picture Tomasz at fifty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'without wrecking their teams'. What does that mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means not doing what I've seen some firms do, where they buy the software, send the email and walk away. I'd want people moved into new roles, trained properly and told the truth early. That's how my parents ran the bakery with their two staff, and it's how I'd want to run any project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomasz about 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my husband Tomasz to start teaching apprentices in his forties, because a person who can train others lasts longer than a person who just does the work. Then I'd tell him not to worry yet, which he wouldn't listen to anyway. He's a planner like me, just with cables instead of spreadsheets.

Ten years is **two career moves** for someone my age, so I'd frame it as a challenge.
think: A decade of firms will need people who bring AI in **without wrecking teams**.
The real worry is **2039**, when robots reach Tomasz's trade and we have kids.
do: **Move** into an AI rollout role, maybe at a consultancy, within three years.
**Buy** a house and try for a **first child** in 2028.
**Top up** my pension with a share of every bonus.
feel: Mostly **positive**, like the wind is behind me for once.

S4.quote: A person who can train others lasts longer than a person who just does the work.
fieldNote: With a decade, she sees her own career as a **winner** from the change and admits feeling guilty.
Her unease is about **Tomasz's trade** in 2039, not her own income.
Her model for change is her parents' **bakery**: retrain, tell the truth early, keep people on.

steps.text: Move into an AI rollout role at a consultancy within three years
Buy a house with Tomasz in 2028
Try for a first child in 2028

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because it's the only one where being early doesn't save you, and we'd have no house and no business ready. What would help is cheap, simple ways for small firms to start, like quick business registration and small start-up loans, and companies paying for retraining before they cut. I'd rather have a fair start than a benefit cheque.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. People assume someone who works with AI every day can't be religious, but Mass on Sunday is the one hour a week no screen is talking to me. I think that hour would matter more, not less, in every one of these pictures.

headlineQuote: Mass on Sunday is the one hour a week no screen is talking to me.
portrait: Priya Kowalski, 27, leads a **six-person demand planning** team at a large home-improvement chain's head office.
She uses **AI every day**, built her own sell-out alert tool, and is seen as the team's early adopter.
Married to **Tomasz**, an electrician, she is saving for a house and wants children within a few years.
Traditional on **family and faith**, she frames retraining as an employer keeping its bargain, not a handout.
She moves from calm to anxious as AGI speeds up, pivoting to an **electrical firm** with Tomasz.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because being early doesn't save her and there's no house or business ready.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap, simple** business registration and small start-up loans for new firms.
Companies paying for **retraining** before they cut jobs.
